title: Thinking Machines
subtitle: A short history of artificial intelligence, 1950 to today

narration: For as long as we have built machines, we have wondered whether they could think.
This is the story of how that question became one of the defining technologies of our time: the setbacks, the breakthroughs, and the ideas that finally worked.

scenes.title: Can machines think?

facts.text: Alan Turing, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”
Proposes the Imitation Game, later called the Turing Test

narration: In 1950, the British mathematician Alan Turing published a paper that opened with a simple question: can machines think?
Rather than define thinking, he proposed a test.
If a machine could hold a conversation that a person couldn't tell apart from a human's, perhaps we should call it intelligent.
He called it the imitation game.

scenes.title: A field gets its name

facts.text: Dartmouth Summer Research Project
McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon coin “artificial intelligence”

narration: Six years later, a small group of researchers gathered at Dartmouth College for a summer workshop.
Their proposal, written by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, gave the field its name: artificial intelligence.
They believed a significant advance could be made in a single summer.
It would take a good deal longer.

scenes.title: The perceptron learns

facts.text: Frank Rosenblatt, Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory
Learns from examples by adjusting connection weights

narration: In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt unveiled the perceptron, a machine loosely modeled on the neurons of the brain.
Instead of following hand-written rules, it learned from examples by adjusting the strength of its connections.
The press predicted it would one day walk, talk, and be conscious of its own existence.
That idea, learning by adjusting connections, would wait decades for its moment.

scenes.title: Intelligence as logic and rules

facts.text: Logic Theorist proves theorems from Principia Mathematica
ELIZA (1966) chats using simple pattern matching
Shakey the robot plans its own actions

narration: Meanwhile, the dominant approach was symbolic: intelligence as the manipulation of logic and rules, and programs soon proved mathematical theorems and solved puzzles.
In 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA imitated a therapist using simple pattern matching, and people confided in it anyway.
At the Stanford Research Institute, a robot named Shakey learned to plan its own moves.

say.1: In 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum's Eliza imitated a therapist using simple pattern matching, and people confided in it anyway.

scenes.title: The first AI winter

facts.text: 1969: Minsky & Papert’s “Perceptrons” exposes single-layer limits
1973: UK Lighthill Report criticizes the field
Funding in the US and UK is cut back sharply

narration: But early promises outran reality: problems that looked simple, like understanding language or recognizing objects, exploded in complexity.
In 1969, Minsky and Papert showed the limits of single-layer perceptrons, and in 1973 the Lighthill Report in Britain criticized the field's failure to deliver.
Funding dried up. This was the first AI winter.

scenes.title: Expert systems and backpropagation

facts.text: Knowledge captured as thousands of IF–THEN rules
XCON configures computer orders at Digital Equipment Corp.
1986: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams popularize backpropagation

narration: In the 1980s, AI returned as expert systems: programs that encoded the knowledge of human specialists as thousands of “if this, then that” rules.
One, called XCON, configured computer orders for Digital Equipment Corporation and saved the company tens of millions of dollars a year.
At the same time, in 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams showed how backpropagation could train neural networks with hidden layers, reviving the idea Rosenblatt had started.

say.1: One, called X-con, configured computer orders for Digital Equipment Corporation and saved the company tens of millions of dollars a year.
say.0: In the 1980s, AI returned as expert systems: programs that encoded the knowledge of human specialists as thousands of "if this, then that" rules.

scenes.title: The second AI winter

facts.text: Rule systems prove brittle and costly to maintain
1987: the specialized Lisp machine market collapses

narration: But expert systems proved brittle and expensive to maintain.
When the market for specialized AI hardware collapsed in 1987, a second AI winter set in, and many researchers avoided the term artificial intelligence altogether.

scenes.title: Quiet progress

facts.text: Yann LeCun’s convolutional networks read handwritten digits
1997: IBM Deep Blue beats Garry Kasparov 3½–2½

narration: Yet progress continued quietly: Yann LeCun's convolutional neural networks learned to read handwritten digits, and were soon reading bank checks.
And in 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, searching around two hundred million positions per second.

say.0: Yet progress continued quietly: Yann Le Kun's convolutional neural networks learned to read handwritten digits, and were soon reading bank checks.

scenes.title: Data and compute arrive

facts.text: The internet generates data on a massive scale
2009: ImageNet, 14 million labeled images
GPUs built for games accelerate neural networks

narration: The 2000s brought the ingredients that had been missing, as the internet produced data on a massive scale.
In 2009, Fei-Fei Li's team released ImageNet, more than fourteen million labeled images.
And graphics chips built for video games turned out to be ideal for the math of neural networks.

say.1: In 2009, Fay-Fay Lee's team released ImageNet, more than fourteen million labeled images.

scenes.title: The deep learning revolution

facts.text: AlexNet: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton
Trained on two consumer gaming GPUs
Error rates fall below the human estimate by 2015

narration: In 2012, these ingredients came together: a deep neural network called AlexNet, built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton and trained on two gaming GPUs, won the ImageNet competition by a stunning margin.
Within three years, deep networks matched human accuracy on that benchmark.
The deep learning revolution had begun.

say.0: In 2012, these ingredients came together: a deep neural network called Alex-Net, built by Alex Kri-zhev-sky, Ilya Suts-kever and Geoffrey Hinton and trained on two gaming G.P.U.s, won the ImageNet competition by a stunning margin.

scenes.title: Deep learning everywhere

facts.text: Breakthroughs in speech recognition and translation
2014: Ian Goodfellow invents GANs
DeepMind’s DQN learns Atari games from raw pixels

narration: Deep learning spread rapidly, transforming speech recognition and machine translation.
In 2014, Ian Goodfellow introduced generative adversarial networks, in which two networks compete: one forging images, the other spotting the fakes.
And DeepMind trained a single network to play dozens of Atari games directly from the pixels on the screen.

scenes.title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol

facts.text: DeepMind’s AlphaGo wins the match 4–1 in Seoul
Learned from human games and from self-play
Game 2, Move 37: a move no human expected

narration: In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol, one of the greatest Go players in the world, four games to one.
Go has more possible positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, far too many to search by brute force.
AlphaGo learned a kind of intuition, from human games and from playing against itself.
Its thirty-seventh move, in game two, was so unexpected that commentators first thought it was a mistake.

say.0: In 2016, DeepMind's Alpha Go defeated Lee Sedol, one of the greatest Go players in the world, four games to one.
say.2: Alpha Go learned a kind of intuition, from human games and from playing against itself.

scenes.title: Attention Is All You Need

facts.text: Vaswani et al., Google: the Transformer architecture
Self-attention: every word looks at every other word
Parallel, fast to train, and it scales

narration: In 2017, a team at Google published a paper titled Attention Is All You Need.
It introduced the Transformer, an architecture that lets every word in a sentence look directly at every other word to work out what matters.
Transformers were fast to train on modern hardware, and they scaled remarkably well.
Almost every major AI system today is built on this idea.

scenes.title: Bigger models, new abilities

facts.text: Trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next word
GPT-3 (2020): 175 billion parameters
Scaling laws: more compute and data, predictably better

narration: Researchers began training Transformers on vast amounts of text, simply to predict the next word.
With GPT-2 in 2019 and GPT-3 in 2020, at a hundred and seventy-five billion parameters, a striking pattern emerged: as models grew larger and saw more data, they improved predictably.
New skills, like translation, summarization and simple reasoning, appeared without being explicitly taught.

say.1: With G P T 2 in 2019 and G P T 3 in 2020, at a hundred and seventy-five billion parameters, a striking pattern emerged: as models grew larger and saw more data, they improved predictably.

scenes.title: AI transforms science

facts.text: AlphaFold 2 predicts protein structures at CASP14
2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Hassabis & Jumper (with David Baker)
2024 Nobel Prize in Physics: Hopfield & Hinton

narration: AI also began to transform science.
In 2020, DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted the three-dimensional shapes of proteins with accuracy rivaling laboratory experiments, a fifty-year-old grand challenge in biology.
Demis Hassabis and John Jumper later shared in the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
That same year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton, for foundational work on neural networks.

say.1: In 2020, DeepMind's Alpha Fold 2 predicted the three-dimensional shapes of proteins with accuracy rivaling laboratory experiments, a fifty-year-old grand challenge in biology.

scenes.title: Generative AI goes public

facts.text: DALL·E 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion turn text into images
November 30: ChatGPT launches
An estimated 100 million users in about two months

narration: In 2022, generative AI reached the public, as systems like DALL·E 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion turned text descriptions into images.
Then, on November 30th, ChatGPT launched: a large language model fine-tuned with human feedback to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
It reached an estimated one hundred million users in about two months, one of the fastest-growing consumer apps in history.

say.0: In 2022, generative AI reached the public, as systems like Dolly 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion turned text descriptions into images.
say.1: Then, on November 30th, Chat G P T launched: a large language model fine-tuned with human feedback to follow instructions and hold a conversation.

scenes.title: The frontier race

facts.text: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini and open-weight Llama
Multimodal: text, images, audio and long documents
2024: the EU AI Act becomes law

narration: A race followed: GPT-4 from OpenAI, Claude from Anthropic, Gemini from Google, and Meta's open-weight Llama models arrived in quick succession.
Models learned to see images, hear speech, and read documents hundreds of pages long.
Governments responded too, and the European Union passed the AI Act, the first comprehensive law regulating artificial intelligence.

say.0: A race followed: G P T 4 from OpenAI, Claude from Anthropic, Gemini from Google, and Meta's open-weight Llama models arrived in quick succession.

scenes.title: Reasoning and agents

facts.text: Reasoning models think step by step before answering
2025: gold-medal level at the International Math Olympiad
Agents use tools, operate computers and write software

narration: Next came models that think before they answer: starting in late 2024, reasoning models were trained to work through hard problems step by step.
In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
And AI became an agent, able to use tools, browse the web, operate a computer, and write and test software on its own, carrying out tasks that take people hours.

scenes.title: Lessons and open questions

facts.text: Breakthroughs = algorithms + data + compute
Open questions: safety, reliability, alignment, fairness

narration: Today, hundreds of millions of people use AI every week.
Looking back, the pattern is clear: ideas that seemed to fail, like neural networks, succeeded once data and computing power caught up.
The open questions now are as big as the breakthroughs: how to make these systems safe, reliable and aligned with human values, and how to share their benefits fairly.
Seventy-six years after Alan Turing asked whether machines can think, we are still debating the answer.
But the question has changed: it is no longer only what machines can do, but what we will choose to do with them.
